title: Signing, TestFlight, App Store & CI/CD
scopeHtml: Scope: Certificates, provisioning profiles, signing, TestFlight, App Store Connect, review guidelines, fastlane, Xcode Cloud, release process.

notes.title: Baseline and the shape of an iOS release
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you sign an AAB with your upload key, Play App Signing re-signs it, you push to a Play Console track (internal, closed, open, production) and staged rollout percentages. On iOS the app is signed with an Apple-issued certificate tied to your team, uploaded to App Store Connect, tested in TestFlight, reviewed by humans and automation, then released (manually, automatically or in a phased rollout).

Baseline. Xcode 16+, Swift 6, iOS 17/18 minimum deployment target. Apple moves the minimum SDK required for uploads every spring (for example "built with Xcode N and the iOS N SDK"); the exact current requirement: verify on developer.apple.com/news. Anything dated in this note is a snapshot.

 Code --> Build (Debug) --> Archive (Release, signed)
                              |
                              v
                      Upload to App Store Connect
                              |
              +---------------+----------------+
              v                                v
     TestFlight (internal <=100,        App Review (submit a version)
      external up to 10,000 w/ beta           |
      review for first build)                 v
                                       Release: manual / auto /
                                       phased (7 days) --> Users
Android iOS
Keystore + upload key Distribution certificate + provisioning profile
Play App Signing Automatic cloud signing in Xcode / App Store Connect managed
applicationId Bundle Identifier (App ID)
versionName / versionCode CFBundleShortVersionString / CFBundleVersion
Play Console tracks TestFlight groups + App Store release
Staged rollout % Phased release (fixed 7-day schedule)
Pre-launch report TestFlight + App Review (human)
Android Vitals / Crashlytics Xcode Organizer / MetricKit / Crashlytics

Real industry examples. Instagram and Uber release weekly via TestFlight internal builds followed by phased releases; many teams run a two-week train with a release branch. Spotify has publicly described continuous TestFlight distribution to employees.

Everyday analogy. Releasing on iOS is shipping through a customs checkpoint: your passport (certificate) and visa (provisioning profile) must match the cargo (app), and an inspector (App Review) may open the boxes.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming you can upload any APK-like artifact. iOS builds are signed .ipa archives produced by Xcode and uploaded via Xcode, Transporter or xcodebuild -exportArchive (verify current CLI).
  • Believing Android's "push live in minutes" speed carries over. App Review adds hours to days, and there is no instant rollback.
  • Not knowing a build must be uploaded before it appears in TestFlight or can be attached to a version.

notes.title: Code signing: certificates, identifiers and provisioning profiles
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. One keystore signs your APK and identity is the application ID. iOS splits trust into four linked pieces; all four must agree or the build fails with errors like "No profiles for 'com.x.app' were found" or "Provisioning profile doesn't include signing certificate".

  1. Certificate (public/private key pair). Proves who signed. Types: Apple Development (run on your own devices) and Apple Distribution (App Store, TestFlight, ad hoc, enterprise-capable under separate programs). The private key lives in the Mac's Keychain; if you lose that Mac without exporting a .p12, you must revoke and create a new certificate. Per team there are limits on active distribution certificates (small numbers; verify exact limits).
  2. App ID / Bundle Identifier (reverse-DNS, e.g. com.example.app). Proves which app. Capabilities (Push, App Groups, Sign in with Apple, Associated Domains) are enabled on the App ID.
  3. Devices (for Development and Ad Hoc profiles): registered by UDID, up to 100 per device family per year per team.
  4. Provisioning profile (.mobileprovision). A signed bundle that links certificate(s) + App ID + devices (if any) + entitlements. It is embedded in the app as embedded.mobileprovision; at install time the OS checks that the signature chain, profile and entitlements match. Profile types: Development, Ad Hoc, App Store, Enterprise (In-House).
 Apple Developer account (team ID: ABCDE12345)
   |-- Certificate (Apple Distribution) <-- private key on your Mac
   |-- App ID  com.example.app  + capabilities (Push, App Groups...)
   |-- Devices (UDIDs) [dev / ad hoc only]
   `-- Provisioning Profile = cert + App ID + devices + entitlements
                 |
                 v
       codesign(app, cert) + embed profile --> .ipa

Entitlements. A plist of rights compiled and signed into the binary. Example:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>aps-environment</key><string>production</string>
  <key>com.apple.developer.associated-domains</key>
  <array><string>applinks:example.com</string></array>
  <key>com.apple.security.application-groups</key>
  <array><string>group.com.example.shared</string></array>
</dict>
</plist>

If the entitlements file asks for a capability the profile lacks, signing fails or the app is killed at launch (amfid rejection in the device log).

Automatic vs manual signing.

  • Automatic ("Automatically manage signing" with a Team): Xcode creates and refreshes certificates and profiles, and registers devices. Fine for individuals and small teams; the default.
  • Manual: you pick the profile per configuration. Used on CI, in large teams, or when you need reproducibility. Xcode also supports cloud-managed distribution signing so CI need not hold the private key (verify current behaviour for Xcode Cloud and App Store Connect API key flows).
  • fastlane match keeps certificates and profiles encrypted in a private git repo (or storage bucket) so every developer and CI machine shares the same ones; the standard way to avoid "works on my Mac".

Build settings that matter: CODE_SIGN_STYLE, CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY, DEVELOPMENT_TEAM, PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER, CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS.

# Inspect what is actually signed in a build
codesign -dvvv --entitlements :- MyApp.app
security cms -D -i MyApp.app/embedded.mobileprovision

Incident patterns.

  • "Certificate expired" (distribution certs last one year) makes CI fail the day it lapses; already-published apps keep working, but new builds cannot be signed.
  • A developer revokes the distribution certificate "to fix" signing and breaks every colleague's and CI's builds.
  • A new capability (e.g., Push) was added to the App ID but the profile was not regenerated: stale profile error.
  • Extensions and frameworks each need their own App ID/profile (widgets, notification service extension); a missing one breaks archive.

Real industry examples. Large teams standardise on fastlane match plus a CI service account with an App Store Connect API key (an .p8 file with key ID and issuer ID), replacing individual Apple ID passwords and 2FA prompts.

Everyday analogy. The certificate is your employee badge, the App ID is the room number, the devices list is the guest list, and the provisioning profile is the signed pass that says "this badge may enter this room for these guests".

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking the provisioning profile equals the certificate. It references the certificate.
  • Committing the .p12/.p8 or profiles to a public repo.
  • Confusing Development and Distribution certificates, and App Store vs Ad Hoc profiles.
  • Android thinking: "I can lose my upload key and reset it." On iOS you revoke and reissue the certificate, but your App ID and bundle identifier are permanent for that app.

notes.title: Build, archive, upload and versioning
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. ./gradlew bundleRelease makes an AAB and you upload via Play Console or the publishing plugin. iOS uses Archive (Product > Archive, or xcodebuild archive) to make an .xcarchive, then export/upload to App Store Connect.

# 1. Archive a Release build
xcodebuild archive \
  -scheme MyApp \
  -configuration Release \
  -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' \
  -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive

# 2. Export a signed .ipa using an options plist
xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist \
  -exportPath build/ipa
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>method</key><string>app-store-connect</string> <!-- older: app-store (verify) -->
  <key>teamID</key><string>ABCDE12345</string>
  <key>uploadSymbols</key><true/>
  <key>signingStyle</key><string>automatic</string>
</dict>
</plist>

Upload can happen inside the export step (destination upload), via Xcode Organizer ("Distribute App"), the Transporter app, xcrun altool (older; being replaced, verify) or fastlane upload_to_testflight / pilot. After upload, App Store Connect runs processing (binary validation, symbol checks, privacy manifest checks); you receive an email within minutes for rejections of the build before review (for example ITMS-90xxx codes such as missing purpose strings or invalid bundle).

Bitcode was removed in Xcode 14, so no recompilation by Apple; the binary you upload is what users run (thinned for devices via app thinning: slicing, on-demand resources).

Version and build numbers.

  • CFBundleShortVersionString (marketing version, 1.4.0): what users see; must increase (or stay equal) for each App Store version; three period-separated integers.
  • CFBundleVersion (build number, 2154): must be unique and increasing per version train for each uploaded build. You can upload many builds for 1.4.0 (build 1, 2, 3...) and pick one for review.
  • In Xcode these are MARKETING_VERSION and CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION. Automate the build number from CI run number or agvtool next-version -all; fastlane: increment_build_number.
  • Android's versionCode is a single global integer; iOS pairs a user-facing version with a build number, and builds are scoped to the version.
// Reading them at runtime (e.g., for support screens)
let info = Bundle.main.infoDictionary
let version = info?["CFBundleShortVersionString"] as? String ?? "?"
let build = info?["CFBundleVersion"] as? String ?? "?"

Build configurations and secrets. Debug/Release (and often Staging) configurations with .xcconfig files supply per-environment values such as API base URL and bundle identifier suffix, the iOS counterpart to product flavors. Do not commit secrets; inject via CI environment.

Swift Package Manager dependencies resolve into Package.resolved; commit it for reproducible CI builds. A cold CI build time is a major cost, so cache DerivedData / SwiftPM caches (verify safe cache keys).

Incident patterns.

  • "The bundle version must be higher than the previously uploaded version": forgot to bump the build number.
  • Archive succeeds but upload fails with a missing icon (alpha channel in the 1024x1024 icon) or missing ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption handling: set the key in Info.plist (false if you only use standard HTTPS) to skip the export-compliance question each time.
  • Debug code or staging URLs shipped because the wrong configuration was archived.

Real industry examples. Airbnb and Lyft generate build numbers from CI job numbers so every artifact is traceable to a commit; Sentry/Crashlytics releases are tagged with version+build.

Everyday analogy. The version is the edition of a book (2nd edition); the build number is the print run. Many print runs may exist for the same edition, but each must carry a new, higher number.

Common interview traps.

  • Reusing a build number within a version (rejected at upload).
  • Archiving a Debug configuration (slow, includes debugging overlays, rejected or flagged).
  • Forgetting ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption.
  • Assuming the uploaded build is reviewed automatically; you must select it for a version and submit.

notes.title: TestFlight: internal and external testing
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Play's internal testing track is instant and open to up to 100 testers; closed and open testing add review. TestFlight is the equivalent, built into App Store Connect, with an iOS app that installs builds for testers.

Internal testing External testing
Who up to 100 members of your App Store Connect team (roles required) up to 10,000 people by email or public link
Review none first build of a version needs Beta App Review (lighter than App Review); later builds of the same version often pass quickly
Availability immediately after processing after beta review approval
Build life 90 days 90 days

(Numbers are from Apple's documentation at the time of writing; verify the current limits.)

Mechanism. After processing, a build can be assigned to groups. Internal groups can auto-distribute every new build. External groups have invite via email or a public link with a tester cap. Testers get "What to Test" notes, can send feedback and screenshots from the TestFlight app, and crash reports flow to App Store Connect. Builds expire after 90 days. TestFlight builds are signed with the distribution profile and are standard App Store binaries, so IAP uses the sandbox environment (verify StoreKit testing details).

# fastlane: upload, distribute to a group, with changelog
fastlane pilot upload \
  --ipa build/ipa/MyApp.ipa \
  --groups "QA, Beta" \
  --changelog "Fixes login crash on iOS 17.5" \
  --skip_waiting_for_build_processing false

Useful practices.

  • Keep an internal group that receives every main-branch build (nightly).
  • Use external beta groups for staged exposure before the App Store; gather crash rate and feedback.
  • For features not ready, use remote feature flags (Firebase Remote Config, LaunchDarkly), because iOS releases cannot be hot-patched.
  • StoreKit configuration files and the sandbox let you test purchases without real money (see the platform frameworks note).

Incident patterns.

  • Testers cannot install: device not eligible for the OS minimum, or the build expired after 90 days.
  • A build stuck in "Processing" for hours; typically resolved by re-uploading, or by Apple status issues (check the developer system status page).
  • Internal testers forget they run a build that points at staging.

Real industry examples. Many consumer apps (Reddit, Duolingo) run public TestFlight links for beta programs; Apple's own Swift Playgrounds uses it. Companies like Spotify auto-ship each commit to an internal "dogfood" group.

Everyday analogy. TestFlight is the staff preview night at a restaurant: employees (internal) walk right in; friends and critics (external) need a quick invitation check first.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing external testing needs no review. The first build per version is reviewed.
  • Mixing up the bundle ID for beta vs production; TestFlight uses the production bundle ID, so people use a separate "Beta" app record only when they want parallel installs.
  • Assuming TestFlight builds never expire.
  • Treating Debug and TestFlight builds as the same environment (receipts, push environments, and entitlements differ).

notes.title: App Review guidelines and common rejection reasons
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Google Play review is mostly automated with policy strikes; Apple's review is human plus automated, driven by the App Store Review Guidelines (sections: 1 Safety, 2 Performance, 3 Business, 4 Design, 5 Legal). Typical timing is within about a day or two for most submissions (not guaranteed; verify), but first submissions and sensitive categories take longer.

Most common rejections, with the guideline family and fix.

Reason Guideline Fix
Crashes, bugs, broken links 2.1 App Completeness test on release build, supply working demo account
Missing or invalid demo credentials, backend down 2.1 provide live review credentials in the review notes
Placeholder content, minimal functionality 4.2 Minimum Functionality add native value beyond a web wrapper
Misleading metadata / screenshots 2.3 match real UI, do not mention other platforms
Digital goods bought outside In-App Purchase 3.1.1 use StoreKit; (external link rules have shifted by region: verify)
Account creation without account deletion in app 5.1.1(v) add in-app delete account flow
Social login offered without Sign in with Apple 4.8 offer SIWA or an equivalent privacy-focused option (rule has been adjusted: verify)
Vague permission strings or over-collection 5.1.1 / 5.1.2 specific usage strings, ask only when needed
Missing privacy policy, wrong privacy labels 5.1.1 policy URL, accurate labels, privacy manifest
Using private APIs 2.5.1 use public APIs only
User-generated content with no reporting/blocking 1.2 add report, block, filter, contact info
Subscription UI lacks price, term, restore 3.1.2 clear price/duration, "Restore Purchases", Terms/Privacy links
Spam / copycat / 4.3 duplicate apps 4.3 differentiate; avoid template clones

Review notes and demo. Use the "App Review Information" box to explain hidden features, hardware dependencies, and give a demo account. For apps needing a backend, keep it up through the review window. If rejected, the Resolution Center message cites the guideline; you can reply, fix and resubmit a new build, or appeal to the App Review Board.

Expedited review can be requested for critical bug fixes (use sparingly). Pre-order, release-on-approval, scheduled release are options at submission.

Other submission chores. Screenshots for required device sizes, an app icon (1024x1024 no alpha), age rating questionnaire, export compliance, content rights, privacy nutrition labels, support URL, and an App Store product page (in-app events and custom product pages exist for marketing; verify current set). Localisation of metadata is per locale.

Incident patterns.

  • Rejection due to the backend returning a 500 or an expired demo account during review.
  • Rejection because a subscription paywall hid the "Restore" button.
  • Binary rejection ITMS-90683 (missing purpose string) and ITMS-91053 (required reason API missing in privacy manifest), see the security note.
  • An update rejected for UGC without moderation tools after a feature launch.

Real industry examples. Epic Games, Spotify and others publicly fought Apple over In-App Purchase rules (guideline 3.1.1 and anti-steering); regional regulations (EU Digital Markets Act alternative distribution, US court rulings) have changed what is allowed. Details change often: verify.

Everyday analogy. App Review is a building inspector: the most common failures are not exotic code violations but missing fire exits (account deletion), unclear signage (permission strings) and doors that do not open when he arrives (broken demo login).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Apple only tests the binary. They read the metadata, privacy answers, screenshots and your review notes too.
  • Offering a feature that "unlocks premium" via web payment inside the app without checking 3.1.1.
  • Not providing demo credentials for an app behind login.
  • Assuming a rejected build can simply be re-submitted unchanged; metadata-only rejections can often be fixed without a new binary, binary rejections need a new build.

notes.title: Phased release, rollout controls and release notes
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Play lets you pick any rollout percentage and halt it. iOS Phased Release for Automatic Updates applies only to users with automatic updates enabled, over a fixed 7-day schedule.

Daily percentages (Apple's published schedule; verify): day 1: 1%, day 2: 2%, day 3: 5%, day 4: 10%, day 5: 20%, day 6: 50%, day 7: 100%. You can pause the phased release for up to 30 days or release to all users immediately. Users who manually update from the App Store can always get the new version at any point (the phase only controls automatic updates). You cannot choose a percentage, and you cannot roll back a version: to undo, you must ship a new version (a higher number) or reuse the previous binary as a new version with a higher build; an old build can be resubmitted only as a new version (verify exact rules). Expedited review helps.

Release options at approval time. Manual release (you press the button), automatic after approval, or scheduled for a date after approval. Phased release is a checkbox on the version.

Minimum-version enforcement ("force update"). Since you cannot halt installs of a broken version already in users' hands, apps implement a remote minimum-version check:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct AppConfig: Decodable, Sendable { let minimumVersion: String }

func needsForcedUpdate(config: AppConfig) -> Bool {
    let current = Bundle.main.infoDictionary?["CFBundleShortVersionString"] as? String ?? "0"
    return current.compare(config.minimumVersion, options: .numeric) == .orderedAscending
}
data class AppConfig(val minimumVersion: String)

fun needsForcedUpdate(config: AppConfig, current: String): Boolean =
    compareVersions(current, config.minimumVersion) < 0
// Android also has Play In-App Updates API (immediate / flexible); iOS has no equivalent,
// you deep-link to https://apps.apple.com/app/id<APP_ID> yourself.

Add remote kill-switches for features (feature flags) to compensate for the lack of rollback.

Release notes ("What's New"). Per locale, up to a few thousand characters; users read the first lines. Do not mention bug IDs; do not reference other platforms. TestFlight has a separate "What to Test" text.

Release train and hotfix flow.

main  ---o---o---o---o---o---o--->
              \
 release/1.4   o--o--(fix)--> submit 1.4.0 (build 3)
                         \
                          `-> hotfix/1.4.1 --> expedited review

Monitor the first 24-48 hours: crash-free users and sessions in Xcode Organizer and Crashlytics, hangs, support tickets. Pause the phased release if the rate dips.

Real industry examples. Instagram and Facebook use server-driven kill-switches; Uber runs "release candidate" builds in TestFlight for a week before phased release. Teams track "adoption curve" dashboards because OS and version adoption informs the minimum deployment target.

Everyday analogy. A phased release is letting a few diners try the new menu each day, but there is no recall once a diner has eaten; so you keep a note on the door (remote flag) that can pull a dish.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a custom rollout percentage or a rollback button like Play Console.
  • Thinking phased release applies to manual updaters.
  • Treating the build number as the marketing version when comparing for forced updates (use the marketing version, with numeric comparison).
  • Forgetting that after "Release to all" you cannot go back to phased.

notes.title: fastlane, Xcode Cloud and GitHub Actions
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android CI runs Gradle on cheap Linux runners and Gradle Play Publisher uploads. iOS builds require macOS (Xcode only runs on Macs), so CI means macOS runners, which are slower and pricier.

fastlane is the Ruby toolchain for iOS automation (also supports Android). Key tools: gym (build/archive), pilot (TestFlight), deliver (metadata, screenshots), match (signing), scan (tests), snapshot (localised screenshots), pem/sigh older helpers.

# fastlane/Fastfile
default_platform(:ios)

platform :ios do
  desc "Build and push to TestFlight"
  lane :beta do
    setup_ci                                   # temp keychain on CI
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"],
      issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"],
      key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_P8"]
    )
    match(type: "appstore", readonly: true, api_key: api_key)
    increment_build_number(build_number: ENV["GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER"])
    build_app(scheme: "MyApp", export_method: "app-store")
    upload_to_testflight(api_key: api_key, skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true)
  end
end

GitHub Actions on macOS runners:

name: ios-beta
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  beta:
    runs-on: macos-15          # pick a runner image that has your Xcode (verify)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Select Xcode
        run: sudo xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode_16.app
      - name: Test
        run: |
          xcodebuild test -scheme MyApp -testPlan Unit \
            -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 15' | xcbeautify
      - name: Ship
        run: bundle exec fastlane beta
        env:
          ASC_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_ID }}
          ASC_ISSUER_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_ISSUER_ID }}
          ASC_KEY_P8: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_P8 }}
          MATCH_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MATCH_PASSWORD }}

Xcode Cloud is Apple's hosted CI/CD integrated into Xcode and App Store Connect. Workflows trigger on branch, PR or tag; actions are build, test, analyze, archive; post-actions notify TestFlight groups or Slack. It manages signing for you (cloud signing), has custom scripts (ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh, ci_pre_xcodebuild.sh) and a monthly free compute-hour allowance on paid developer programs (amount: verify). Trade-offs: easy signing and tight TestFlight integration versus less flexibility than GitHub Actions or Bitrise, and tied to Apple's supported Xcode and runner versions.

Option Strengths Weaknesses
Xcode Cloud zero signing pain, integrated fewer integrations, Apple-controlled images
GitHub Actions + fastlane flexible, familiar, matrix builds macOS minutes expensive, you maintain signing
Bitrise / CircleCI / Codemagic mobile-optimised steps, caching vendor cost
Self-hosted Mac minis fast and cheap at scale maintenance, security patching

CI pitfalls. Temporary keychains (setup_ci) so codesign can access certificates non-interactively; pinned Xcode and simulator versions; Package.resolved committed; caching; secrets via the App Store Connect API key rather than a personal Apple ID, which requires 2FA.

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Lyft and Uber run large Mac fleets with distributed build caches (Bazel at Uber/Lyft/Pinterest); smaller teams standardise on GitHub Actions + fastlane, or Xcode Cloud for simplicity.

Everyday analogy. CI is a factory line: fastlane is the standard recipe card, the runner is the physical worker (a Mac), and the signing keys are the factory's seal that must be handed to each worker safely.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a personal Apple ID password in CI instead of an API key.
  • Letting the CI keychain prompt for access (job hangs forever).
  • Not pinning the Xcode version, so a runner image update breaks builds.
  • Assuming macOS runners cost the same as Linux ones.

notes.title: Crash reporting: Organizer, Crashlytics, dSYMs and symbolication
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android, R8 produces mapping.txt which Play Console and Crashlytics use to de-obfuscate stack traces. On iOS the equivalent is the dSYM (debug symbols bundle) which maps memory addresses in crash logs back to function names and line numbers. Without it, a crash shows only hex addresses.

Thread 0 Crashed:
0   MyApp    0x0000000104a1c3f4 0x104a00000 + 115700     <- unsymbolicated
0   MyApp    ProfileViewModel.load(id:) + 84 (ProfileViewModel.swift:42)  <- symbolicated

Sources of crash data.

  • Xcode Organizer > Crashes: aggregated, symbolicated crash reports from users who opted into sharing diagnostics (App Store and TestFlight builds), grouped by signature, with the number of devices and the OS versions. Also Energy, Hangs, Launch time, Disk writes, Memory, Terminations metrics.
  • MetricKit (MXMetricManager): in-app delivery of daily metrics and diagnostic payloads (crash, hang, CPU exception, disk write exception) that you can upload to your backend.
  • Third-party SDKs: Firebase Crashlytics, Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog. They catch signals/Mach exceptions and uncaught Objective-C exceptions, add breadcrumbs, user IDs and non-fatal errors.
import MetricKit

final class MetricsSubscriber: NSObject, MXMetricManagerSubscriber {
    func didReceive(_ payloads: [MXDiagnosticPayload]) {
        for p in payloads {
            // p.crashDiagnostics, p.hangDiagnostics, ...
            // Forward p.jsonRepresentation() to your backend (verify API shape)
        }
    }
}
// register once at launch: MXMetricManager.shared.add(subscriber)

dSYM mechanics. The build produces MyApp.app.dSYM when "Debug Information Format" is "DWARF with dSYM File" (Release default). The dSYM is matched by the build's UUID (dwarfdump --uuid). When you upload to App Store Connect with "Upload symbols" enabled, Apple holds the dSYM for Organizer. For Crashlytics you must upload dSYMs yourself, via a Run Script build phase with the Firebase run script or upload-symbols, or fastlane upload_symbols_to_crashlytics. A classic incident: a release crashes massively but Crashlytics shows unsymbolicated frames because the dSYMs were not uploaded; a common cause is that the dSYMs stayed on the CI machine or in the Xcode Cloud artifact (download them from Organizer or App Store Connect to recover).

# Check which UUIDs a dSYM contains and match to the crash log's Binary Images
dwarfdump --uuid MyApp.app.dSYM

# Manually symbolicate one address (arm64)
atos -arch arm64 -o MyApp.app.dSYM/Contents/Resources/DWARF/MyApp \
     -l 0x104a00000 0x0000000104a1c3f4

Reading a crash log. Key fields: Exception Type (EXC_BAD_ACCESS, EXC_CRASH (SIGABRT), EXC_BREAKPOINT for Swift runtime traps like force-unwrapping nil, array index out of range, or integer overflow), Termination Reason (for example 0x8badf00d is a watchdog kill: the app blocked the main thread too long during launch/resume; 0xdead10cc means holding a file lock or SQLite database in a shared container when suspending; 0xc00010ff is thermal), and the Triggered by Thread backtrace. Meaning of codes and exact format: verify per OS version.

Production patterns. Crash-free users above about 99.5% is a common target (a team convention, not an Apple figure). Track by version and OS, and by "hang rate" (main thread unresponsive over a threshold) as hangs are invisible to crash SDKs unless using MetricKit or Sentry's app-hang detection. Out-of-memory kills (jetsam) leave no crash log; infer them with heuristics (the previous session ended without a clean exit).

Real industry examples. Instagram's and Facebook's mobile teams developed FBAllocationTracker and OOM detection heuristics; Sentry and Crashlytics both publish out-of-memory detection approaches. Apple's Organizer is the only source with data from users who never opened your app after install, as it comes from the OS.

Everyday analogy. The crash log without dSYM is a ransom note written in room numbers; the dSYM is the hotel directory that tells you which person (function) lives in each room (address).

Common interview traps.

  • Not uploading dSYMs for each release (or uploading ones from a different build, wrong UUID).
  • Reading EXC_BREAKPOINT as a hardware fault; it is typically a Swift runtime trap (force unwrap, precondition failure).
  • Expecting Crashlytics to report jetsam/OOM kills as crashes.
  • Confusing a watchdog kill (0x8badf00d) with a code crash: look at the main thread's stack for blocking I/O or a deadlock.

notes.title: Enterprise, ad hoc distribution and Play Console comparison
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you can sideload an APK anywhere. On iOS outside the App Store, distribution is limited and gated by Apple programs.

Channel Who Limits
Development install your team registered devices (100 per type per year), profile expires after 1 year
Ad Hoc QA, small groups up to 100 registered UDIDs per device type per year; profile valid 1 year
TestFlight testers see earlier section, 90-day builds
Apple Business Manager / Custom Apps private apps for organisations distributed via the App Store privately to named organisations (verify current naming)
Enterprise Program (In-House) large companies, internal employees only requires 100+ employee organisation; misuse (public distribution) leads to certificate revocation
Unlisted app distribution app reachable only by direct link App Store review still applies
Alternative marketplaces / web distribution EU (Digital Markets Act) and some regions regional and conditional; verify current rules

Ad Hoc mechanics. Add device UDIDs to the portal, regenerate the Ad Hoc profile, archive with that profile and export with method: ad-hoc, then distribute the .ipa (via a service like Firebase App Distribution, Diawi, or a manifest plist over HTTPS using itms-services://). Firebase App Distribution is the common QA channel across both platforms.

MDM-managed installs. Companies push apps through Mobile Device Management (Jamf, Intune), using Apple Business Manager for volume purchasing, supervised devices and managed app configuration (com.apple.configuration.managed in UserDefaults).

// Managed App Configuration read by an enterprise app
let managed = UserDefaults.standard.dictionary(forKey: "com.apple.configuration.managed")
let server = managed?["serverURL"] as? String

Enterprise cautions. Apple has revoked enterprise certificates from companies (Facebook's "Research" app and Google's Screenwise in 2019) for distributing to consumers; all apps signed by that certificate stopped launching. Enterprise distribution is strictly for employees.

Side by side with Play Console.

Topic Play Console App Store Connect
Staged rollout any % fixed 7-day phased release
Halt halt anytime pause up to 30 days; no rollback
Test tracks internal/closed/open TestFlight internal/external
Signing Play App Signing holds app key you manage certs/profiles; Apple re-signs App Store builds
Review time hours to days, mostly automated typically about a day, human-involved
Sideloading open restricted (ad hoc, enterprise, regional alt-distribution)
Crash vitals Android Vitals Organizer, MetricKit
Deobfuscation mapping.txt dSYM

Real industry examples. Banks and airlines use Apple Business Manager custom apps for staff; startups use Ad Hoc via Firebase App Distribution for early QA; Facebook and Google's 2019 enterprise certificate revocations are the standard cautionary tale.

Everyday analogy. The App Store is a licensed shopping mall; Ad Hoc is handing a few friends a sample from your car; Enterprise is a staff canteen that is not allowed to sell to the public.

Common interview traps.

  • Telling a client "just send them the IPA" without UDIDs registered.
  • Using an Enterprise certificate for external beta users (violates the program, revocation risk).
  • Not knowing profiles expire (Development/Ad Hoc after a year) so QA builds suddenly stop launching.
  • Assuming sideloading rules are the same worldwide; regional regulation has changed and keeps changing (verify).

notes.title: Putting it together: a release checklist
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you bump versionCode, build an AAB, upload to a track, and roll out. The iOS list has more gates because Apple owns more of the pipeline.

  1. Cut release/x.y.z; freeze features; set MARKETING_VERSION.
  2. CI archives a Release configuration with the distribution profile; build number from CI run.
  3. Upload to App Store Connect; wait for processing; fix any ITMS email errors (privacy manifest, purpose strings, icons).
  4. Distribute to internal TestFlight; run smoke tests on a real device (not only the Simulator) and an older supported OS.
  5. Promote to external beta if needed; collect Organizer crash data on the beta build.
  6. Complete metadata: What's New per locale, screenshots, privacy labels, age rating, export compliance, review notes with demo credentials.
  7. Submit for review; choose release option and phased release.
  8. After approval: release; monitor crash-free rate, hangs, launch time; pause phased release on regression.
  9. Archive dSYMs, tag the commit (git tag v1.4.0-2154), and publish release notes internally.
  10. Hotfix path: branch, bump patch version, expedited review request, remote flags in the meantime.

A tiny, testable helper that CI can use to guard the version rule:

import Foundation

func isValidTrain(marketing: String, build: String) -> Bool {
    let parts = marketing.split(separator: ".")
    return (1...3).contains(parts.count)
        && parts.allSatisfy { Int($0) != nil }
        && Int(build) != nil
}

Real industry examples. Many teams script this with fastlane lanes (lane :release) and a checklist in the PR template; Slack bots announce App Store Connect status changes through the App Store Connect API webhooks (verify).

Everyday analogy. Releasing is a flight: pre-flight checks (build, test), boarding (upload and TestFlight), air traffic clearance (review), and a cautious descent (phased rollout) with the cockpit instruments (Organizer) watched throughout.

Common interview traps.

  • Skipping real-device testing of the Release configuration (Simulator hides signing, entitlement and performance issues).
  • Forgetting to archive dSYMs and tag the release.
  • Missing a metadata-only requirement (privacy labels) discovered at submission time.
  • Planning a Friday release without time for review and a possible rejection.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• iOS signing = certificate (who) + App ID (which app) + devices (where, dev/ad hoc) + provisioning profile (the signed link) + entitlements; use automatic signing for small teams and fastlane match plus API keys for CI.
  • Archive a Release build, export or upload to App Store Connect; CFBundleShortVersionString is the user version, CFBundleVersion must be unique and increasing per version; set ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption.
  • TestFlight: internal (up to 100, no review) and external (up to 10,000, first build beta-reviewed), builds expire in 90 days.
  • App Review is human and policy-heavy; top rejections are crashes, missing demo credentials, 3.1.1 payments, missing account deletion, vague permission strings and privacy mismatches.
  • Phased release is a fixed 7-day schedule for automatic updaters, pausable but not rollback-able; use remote feature flags and a minimum-version check as safety nets.
  • CI needs macOS: fastlane, GitHub Actions or Xcode Cloud, with temp keychains, pinned Xcode and an App Store Connect API key.
  • Upload dSYMs for every release; read crash logs for EXC_BREAKPOINT, 0x8badf00d watchdog and 0xdead10cc; use Organizer and MetricKit for field data.
  • Ad hoc, enterprise and custom-app distribution each have strict limits; enterprise certificates are for employees only, and regional rules for alternative distribution change (verify).
